candidates.title: SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (photos)
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought. The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13) It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19 , which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a ship at sea shortly after the Oct. 12 launch. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28. Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14 , and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites , all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said. Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy , in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase. That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions. Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. SpaceX and NASA are preparing to fly a resupply cargo flight to the International Space Station on Tuesday morning. The pre-sunrise launch will be SpaceX’s 35th mission to the orbiting outpost as part of NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services (CRS) contract. Liftoff of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 6:33 a.m. EDT (1033 UTC). The rocket will fly on a northeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad. If all goes well, the Cargo Dragon spacecraft, tail number C211, will dock with the zenith port of the Harmony module on Oct. 15 around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 UTC). The space-facing docking port was recently vacated by the Crew Dragon Freedom , which safely delivered the four members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission back to Earth with a splashdown on Oct. 8. candidates.title: Astronomers witness supermassive black hole gorge on a cosmic meal before 'burping' radio jets 300 days later
candidates.raw_excerpt: Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter. Actively feeding supermassive black holes sit in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with their immense gravity heating surrounding matter, causing them to glow brightly. These emissions are boosted by material channeled to the poles of the central black hole, from where it is blasted out as powerful twin jets that shine across the electromagnetic spectrum , particularly in radio waves. The observation of the following radio jet from the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275 via flaring in radio waves is crucial for understanding the relationship between the disk of matter that surrounds and feeds the black hole, called an accretion disk, and the jets it launches. This so-called disk-jet coupling is key to developing a better picture of how black holes influence star formation in the galaxies in which they sit, and thus the growth of those galaxies. Making these observations is no mean feat. The ideal spacecraft for observing X-ray emissions is Chandra , but it doesn't observe NGC 1275 frequently enough to observe its long-term behaviour. NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory may lack the power of Chandra, but having launched in 2004, it has collected a vast amount of data regarding NGC 1275 and its central supermassive black hole. The second task order, Delivery Order 3 (DO3), York will support part of an in-orbit demonstration. candidates.title: Planet Introduces Map of World’s Population With Microsoft and IHME
candidates.raw_excerpt: Planet has debuted a new, continuously updated map of the world’s population built through a collaboration with the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington and Microsoft ‘s AI for Good Lab. The map, called Populace, brings together satellite imagery, machine learning models, and outside data to provide population density at a gridded resolution of 40 meters around the entire world that is updated quarterly. Planet called it the most up-to-date, highest resolution, and most accurate population data. Planet announced the new map on Oct. 12. Populace came about from a collaboration between Planet, IMHE, and the AI for Good Lab that began in 2024. Planet explained the map uses Planet’s satellite imagery basemaps of the Planet, analyzed by AI for Good machine learning models to detect human structures. IMHE then compares that data against census, survey, and administrative data for reliable population estimates. The goal of the project was to use up-to-date satellite information to fill in the gaps where census information is out of date or not available when populations are growing quickly. Planet said this data can be used for planning purposes like public health and civil infrastructure, as well as humanitarian responses and emergency warning. “Climate change, rapid urbanization, migration and emerging infectious diseases are reshaping who is at risk, and where. We cannot address risks we cannot see. Populace gives the global health community a far more timely and granular foundation for understanding those risks – and that kind of data is exactly what we need to protect lives in the decades ahead,” commented Christopher Murray, Professor at the University of Washington and Director of IHME. The product is free of charge for nonprofit organizations and academic researchers, while governments and private-sector organizations will be able to access Populace under commercial-use terms. candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and permanently shadowed regions," the agency wrote, referring to deeply cratered areas where the sun does not touch the lunar surface. The concern is that astronauts' spacesuits could become electrically charged, as there would be an excess of electrons (negatively charged particles) compared with ions (positively charged) in these areas. "The risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft," the agency added. The lander would have a slight positive charge, producing an issue once the "highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle." NASA has asked industry partners for ideas that can help an astronaut avoid "becoming a walking, high voltage capacitor", including issues such as an electrical arc that could damage spacesuits, spark fires in the oxygen atmosphere of a spacecraft, or create electrical shocks. (A Mars simulation in 2018 was reportedly derailed due to a crew experiencing electrical issues, so this problem is not unprecedented.) candidates.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
candidates.raw_excerpt: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November. That's why they're known informally by skywatchers as the "Halloween fireballs." The broad overlapping peaks make the Taurids less about watching on one particular night and more about keeping an eye on the night sky for several weeks. Both have their radiant points — the place in the night sky where their "shooting stars" appear to come from — close to the famous Pleiades (M45) open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus . There's another tempting reason to watch the Taurids in 2026 — moonlight will cause little interference around the main peaks. When are the Southern Taurids? The Southern Taurids are already underway. According to the American Meteor Society , they're active from Sept. 20 through Nov. 20, with two distinct components. The annual component peaks around Oct. 14, while a component particularly associated with fireballs peaks overnight on Nov. 4-5. That's the night to circle if you're hoping to see one of the "Halloween Fireballs." However, don't expect a conventional meteor storm . The Southern Taurids have an average zenithal hourly rate of about five meteors per hour. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space. The crew included Vladimir Komarov (commander), Konstantin Feoktistov (engineer) and Boris Yegorov (doctor), shown at right. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Why it mattered Voskhod 1 served as yet another first for the Soviet Union during a space race kicked off by the launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957 and followed up by the first human spaceflight with Yuri Gagarin in 1961. And while the United States did follow up with its one human spaceflights, until Oct. 12, 1964, every mission had one person on board. That changed with Voskhod 1, which crammed three man into a spacecraft not much larger than the Soviet Union's one-person Vostok spacecraft. At the time, NASA was develoing the two-person Gemini spacecraft , which prompted the Soviet Union's then leader to push for an edge. candidates.raw_excerpt: Beneath its pock-marked, craggy exterior, the Moon is thought to harbor a network of caves and tunnels from its volcanic past. Now, NASA has selected a mission to go investigate a promising window into our space rock’s subterranean secrets. Gaping up at outer space, as if mugging for the orbital satellite cameras, is the Marius Hill Pit, a hole on the lunar surface that’s thought to be up to 150 feet deep and up to 300 feet across. Scientists believe it’s an example of a skylight — the collapsed roof of an underground lava tube , which forms a circular aperture in the ground. If the feature is indeed a skylight, it could give scientists a peek at the Moon’s volcanic history. But scientists are also intrigued by the possibility of using these underground cavities as shelters for astronauts, or even the location of lunar bases. Until now, the hole has only been investigated from orbit. The Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation (GIMLI) aims to do so from the ground.  To determine if the hole opens up into a larger cave, the scientists at the Planetary Science Institute will equip a lunar rover with specialized instruments, including ground penetrating radar, seismic probes, and a sensor that measures the strength of the gravitational field called a gravimeter, to investigate it from the Moon’s surface. The rover will also use cameras to image the exposed portions of the pit. “Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon,” said Gareth Morgan, a Planetary Science Institute senior scientist and deputy principal investigator on the GIMLI program, in a statement . Most of the instruments will be constructed by Honeybee Robotics. candidates.raw_excerpt: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit. The Sentinel-2 pair observe and capture imagery of our planet in different wavelengths using a high-resolution multispectral imager that can see 13 different spectral bands, or ranges of wavelengths. By looking at our planet from space, and observing it through different wavelengths and colors, we can better understand Earth's topography and how it changes over time. With this image, researchers can better understand this landmark in Namibia, a nation in southwestern Africa. Why is it incredible? While this image is strikingly beautiful, the Etosha Pan doesn't exactly look like this in real life. If you were standing close to the pan in the national park, it would look bright white. While this is a real image, false color has been added, which allows scientists to separate different types of vegetation and topography. With the false color, the vegetation surrounding the salt pan appears in shades of red, while the salt pan itself looks like a mix of bright, light and dark blues with cloudy sediment floating around. candidates.raw_excerpt: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history. That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere , trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast.
